lead: No natural product has grade A evidence in irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). For peppermint oil and soluble fibre (psyllium), meta-analyses found each more effective than placebo for overall symptoms, but placebo-controlled peppermint oil trials published in 2020 and 2021 missed their main endpoints and a 2022 review of peppermint oil rated the quality of its evidence very low (both grade B). Probiotic results differ by strain and certainty is mostly low (grade B); wheat bran, prebiotics overall, ginger and St John's wort did no better than placebo.

grade_key.A: Meta-analysis, or at least 2 randomized trials with low risk of bias and a consistent benefit
grade_key.B: 1 good randomized trial, or several randomized trials with mixed results
grade_key.C: Observational studies, small pilots or open-label trials only
grade_key.Negative: Randomized trials found no benefit over placebo

disclaimer: This page summarizes published research. It is not medical advice. Talk to a clinician before starting any supplement, especially if you take other medicines.

products.name: Aloe vera
products.summary: Results are mixed. A 2018 meta-analysis of 3 randomized trials in 151 people found better symptom scores and response rates with aloe vera than with placebo, but a 2026 meta-analysis of 3 studies found no significant difference and said the quality of many studies was limited. Individual trials were mostly null: a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial that randomised 58 people found no evidence of benefit at 1 month, with only a trend in diarrhoea-predominant patients; a crossover trial that randomised 110 people, of whom 47 completed it, found no difference in quality of life; and a randomized, double-blind trial completed by 160 people with all IBS subtypes found aloe extract no better than an inulin control after 4 weeks.
products.safety_interactions: The 2018 meta-analysis found no adverse events related to aloe vera in the included trials. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited studies.

general_safety.name: Aloe vera
general_safety.short: Oral aloe is linked to diarrhoea, low potassium and kidney failure; a case report describes hepatitis. Whole leaf extract is classed as a possible human carcinogen (rat data).

products.name: Anise oil
products.summary: In a three-armed, double-blind trial, 120 people with IBS were randomized to enteric-coated anise oil capsules, placebo or an active control for 4 weeks. At the end, 75% of the anise oil group, 35% of the placebo group and 52.5% of the active-control group were free of IBS symptoms. A 2020 review of herbal medicines noted that the positive herbal trials other than those of peppermint oil, aloe vera and asafoetida have not been replicated. The abstract does not report results by IBS subtype.
products.safety_interactions: No safety data found in the cited trials.

products.name: Berberine
products.summary: One randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial studied berberine on its own, in diarrhoea-predominant IBS. In it, 132 people took 400 mg of berberine hydrochloride a day or placebo for 8 weeks; diarrhoea, abdominal pain and urgency became less frequent with berberine than with placebo. A 2026 meta-analysis of 19 trials in 1,489 people looked at berberine combined with brain-gut axis-targeted medicines for diarrhoea-predominant IBS, not berberine alone; it reported higher response rates with the combinations but judged the overall strength of evidence insufficient because of small samples and methodological weaknesses. No trials in constipation-predominant or mixed IBS were found in PubMed searches on 25 November 2026.
products.safety_interactions: The 132-person trial described berberine as well tolerated, and the 2026 meta-analysis found no serious adverse events reported in the included trials. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited abstracts.

general_safety.name: Berberine
general_safety.short: No serious adverse reactions in a meta-analysis of 27 trials. A review advises caution in pregnancy, newborns and G6PD deficiency, and with medicines metabolised by CYP enzymes.

products.name: Curcumin with fennel oil
aliases: turmeric extract with fennel essential oil
products.summary: In a placebo-controlled trial, 121 people with mild-to-moderate IBS were randomly assigned to capsules combining curcumin and fennel essential oil or to placebo for 30 days. Symptom severity scores fell more with the combination, and 25.9% of that group were symptom-free at the end compared with 6.8% on placebo. In a later open pilot study without a control group, 211 people (14% diarrhoea-predominant, 24% constipation-predominant, 62% mixed) reported lower symptom severity after two months; this is a within-group change. A 2020 review of herbal medicines noted that this positive trial has not been replicated.
products.safety_interactions: The 121-person trial described the combination as safe and well tolerated, without listing adverse events in its abstract. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited studies.

general_safety.name: Turmeric and curcumin
general_safety.short: Case series link turmeric supplements to liver injury, sometimes severe. Curcumin may alter levels of some drugs, including anticoagulants, mostly in non-clinical studies.

general_safety.name: Fennel oil
general_safety.short: Evidence is for fennel preparations in general: trials rarely assessed adverse events and reported no serious ones. A review flags potential interactions with cardiovascular medicines.

products.name: Glutamine
products.summary: The main trial studied a narrow group: adults with diarrhoea-predominant IBS and increased intestinal permeability that began after a gut infection. In this randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 106 people completed 8 weeks of glutamine (5 g three times a day) or placebo; 79.6% of the glutamine group and 5.8% of the placebo group had a drop of at least 50 points in symptom severity score. The authors said large trials should now be done to validate the findings. A second randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial enrolled 50 people with IBS on a low-FODMAP diet and added glutamine (15 g a day) or placebo for 6 weeks; 88% of the glutamine group and 60% of the control group improved by more than 45%.
products.safety_interactions: In the post-infection trial, adverse events and discontinuations were low and similar with glutamine and placebo, and no serious adverse events were observed. The second trial also observed no serious adverse events. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited studies.

general_safety.name: Glutamine
general_safety.short: No adverse effects in a placebo-controlled trial in older adults. A review says it can cause kidney damage in diabetic kidney disease; long-term safety data are limited.

products.name: Melatonin
products.summary: A 2026 systematic review found seven randomized trials in 391 people; pooling four of them, melatonin reduced moderate-to-severe IBS symptoms and pain frequency compared with placebo, with no significant difference in quality of life or sleep quality, and the authors called for larger, high-quality trials. An earlier meta-analysis pooled 4 trials with only 115 participants. In a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 40 people with IBS and sleep disturbances, 3 mg at bedtime for two weeks lowered abdominal pain scores more than placebo, with no difference in bloating or stool frequency. A double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 136 people tested 6 mg a day for 8 weeks; its abstract reports improved IBS scores in people with and without sleep disorders and better quality of life than with placebo. The abstracts do not report results by IBS subtype.
products.safety_interactions: The 2026 review found reported adverse effects were mild and infrequent, and the earlier meta-analysis found a safety profile similar to placebo. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited studies.

general_safety.name: Melatonin
general_safety.short: Trial adverse events were few and mostly mild (daytime sleepiness, headache, dizziness); long-term data are limited. Drugs acting on CYP1A2 may slow its breakdown.

products.name: Nine-herb preparation (bitter candytuft combination)
products.summary: In a double-blind, placebo-controlled, multi-centre trial, 208 people with IBS were randomly assigned to a preparation of nine plant extracts, a six-extract version, bitter candytuft extract alone, or placebo. At 4 weeks both combinations had reduced abdominal pain scores and IBS symptom scores significantly more than placebo; bitter candytuft alone did not differ from placebo. A 2020 review of herbal medicines noted that the positive herbal trials other than those of peppermint oil, aloe vera and asafoetida have not been replicated. The abstract does not report results by IBS subtype.
products.safety_interactions: No safety data found in the cited trials.

general_safety.name: Nine-herb preparation (bitter candytuft combination)
general_safety.short: A review reported adverse drug reactions in 0.04% across various studies, but a case report describes severe acute hepatitis and notes occasional liver-injury cases. No interaction data were found.

products.name: Peppermint oil
products.summary: A 2022 meta-analysis of 10 randomized trials in 1,030 people found peppermint oil more effective than placebo for overall IBS symptoms and abdominal pain, but rated the quality of evidence very low. An earlier meta-analysis of 9 trials of enteric-coated capsules in 726 people also found a benefit and judged the risk of bias low for most factors. Two later placebo-controlled trials were less favourable: a double-blind trial of 190 people found no significant difference in abdominal pain response or overall relief after 8 weeks, although the small-intestinal-release form did better than placebo on secondary measures of pain, discomfort and severity; and a 6-week double-blind trial at a single US centre found no significant differences between peppermint oil and placebo. A 2020 network meta-analysis ranked peppermint oil first for overall symptoms but warned of considerable uncertainty, with few trials at low risk of bias. The abstracts do not report results by IBS subtype.
products.safety_interactions: In the 2022 meta-analysis, adverse events were significantly more frequent with peppermint oil than with placebo. The 2014 meta-analysis found adverse events were mild and transient, and that heartburn was the most commonly reported. In the 190-person trial, adverse events were mild but more common in both peppermint oil groups. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited studies.

general_safety.name: Peppermint oil
general_safety.short: In IBS trials adverse events were more frequent than with placebo but mild and transient; heartburn was most common. A review lists peppermint among supplements linked to bleeding risk.

products.name: Probiotics
products.summary: Results are strain-specific and the certainty is mostly low. A 2023 meta-analysis of 82 randomized trials in 10,332 people concluded that some combinations or strains may be beneficial, with moderate certainty for Escherichia strains on overall symptoms and low to very low certainty for almost everything else; only 24 trials were at low risk of bias across all domains. A 2026 strain-by-strain meta-analysis of placebo-controlled trials found efficacy for Bifidobacterium longum 35624, Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG, Lactiplantibacillus plantarum 299v, Saccharomyces cerevisiae CNCM I-3856 and Bacillus coagulans Unique IS2, but not for Escherichia coli Nissle 1917, Lactobacillus gasseri BNR17 or Lactobacillus casei Shirota. The 2023 review had reported moderate-certainty evidence of benefit for Escherichia strains, and its abstract does not name the strain. A 2026 meta-analysis of 40 studies found improved symptom severity scores but no significant change in quality of life, and rated certainty low because of inconsistency. A 2023 network meta-analysis found four strains and one mixture reduced bowel movement frequency in diarrhoea-predominant IBS.
products.safety_interactions: In the 2023 meta-analysis, the risk of any adverse event, pooled from 55 trials in more than 7,000 people, was not significantly higher with probiotics than with placebo. A 2018 meta-analysis also found adverse events were no more common with probiotics. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited studies.

general_safety.name: Probiotics
general_safety.short: Trials have not shown increased risk, though safety reporting is weak. Rare bloodstream infections occur, mainly in people who are severely ill, immunosuppressed or in intensive care.

products.name: Soluble fibre (psyllium, ispaghula)
products.summary: A 2026 meta-analysis of 30 randomized trials in 1,904 people with IBS found that, in the 16 trials (1,293 people) that reported clinical response, 52% responded to fibre supplements and 44% to control, with a benefit for psyllium specifically; pooled symptom scores did not differ significantly, and results could not be broken down by IBS subtype for most outcomes. A 2014 meta-analysis of 14 trials in 906 people found the benefit only in trials of soluble fibre, and a 2015 meta-analysis reached the same conclusion while noting a moderate risk of bias. In a 12-week primary-care trial of 275 people, more responded to 10 g of psyllium than to placebo in the first month (57% versus 35%) and the second month; quality of life did not differ.
products.safety_interactions: No safety data found in the cited trials.

general_safety.name: Psyllium husk
general_safety.short: Case reports: blockage of the gullet or bowel, with a warning about taking it without adequate fluid, and severe allergic reactions (anaphylaxis) in sensitised people.

products.name: Vitamin D
products.summary: Results are mixed. Five meta-analyses published in 2022 and 2023 disagreed: three found better IBS symptom severity scores with vitamin D than with placebo, and two, including one of 6 trials in 616 people, found no significant effect on symptom severity but a better quality-of-life score. One of the reviews listed small samples, young participants and varied dosing as limitations. A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 135 people in the UK, 60% of whom had low vitamin D at the start, tested 3,000 IU a day for 12 weeks and found no difference in symptom severity or quality of life. The abstracts do not report results by IBS subtype.
products.safety_interactions: One 2022 meta-analysis described a good safety profile for vitamin D supplementation in the included trials. Specific adverse events and interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited abstracts.

general_safety.name: Vitamin D
general_safety.short: Long-term supplementation raised the risk of high blood calcium and high urine calcium in trials, but not kidney stones; toxicity from extremely high doses is rare but serious.

products.name: Artichoke leaf extract
products.summary: No randomized trial of artichoke leaf extract in IBS was found in PubMed searches on 25 November 2026. Two uncontrolled analyses exist, both in people who were taking the extract for indigestion. In a post-marketing surveillance study, a sub-group with IBS symptoms reported less severe symptoms after 6 weeks. In a subset analysis of an open postal study, 208 adults identified afterwards as having IBS were compared before and after two months; the proportion meeting IBS criteria fell by 26.4%. Both are within-group changes with no placebo comparison, and the authors of the first said a controlled trial was justified.
products.safety_interactions: The surveillance study reported that tolerability was very good, without listing adverse events in its abstract. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited studies.

general_safety.name: Artichoke leaf extract
general_safety.short: Limited data from three trials suggest only mild, transient and infrequent adverse events with short-term use. No interaction data were found.

products.name: Pine bark extract
products.summary: The only study found in PubMed searches on 25 November 2026 was a registry study, not described as randomized or blinded, of 77 otherwise healthy people with IBS symptoms. Three groups took the extract (150 mg a day) or one of two other medicines used when needed, for 3 weeks. The number of painful attacks was comparable in all groups; pain on pressing the abdomen improved more in the extract group. There was no placebo group, and the abstract does not report IBS subtype.
products.safety_interactions: No safety data found in the cited trials.

general_safety.name: Pine bark extract
general_safety.short: A systematic review of 15 small trials (791 participants) could draw no definitive conclusions about safety. No interaction data were found.

products.name: Turmeric and curcumin (alone)
products.summary: No placebo-controlled trial of turmeric (Curcuma longa) or curcumin on its own in IBS was found in PubMed searches on 25 November 2026. A 2018 meta-analysis of three studies in 326 people found a beneficial but not statistically significant effect on IBS symptoms and called the evidence limited and heterogeneous. In a partially blinded pilot study, 207 volunteers were randomized to one or two tablets of turmeric extract a day for 8 weeks with no placebo group; about two thirds reported improvement, a within-group change, with no difference between doses. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of a different Curcuma species, Curcuma xanthorrhiza, found no benefit over placebo after 18 weeks. A 30-day trial that randomized 67 people with IBS and small bowel dysbiosis to a low-FODMAP diet with or without a curcumin and boswellia extract reported less bloating and abdominal pain with the supplement; there was no placebo. A 2024 systematic review of turmeric in digestive disorders judged most studies to be at high risk of bias.
products.safety_interactions: The 2018 meta-analysis stated that no adverse events were reported in the available trials, and the 2024 systematic review's descriptive summaries suggested turmeric is safe. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited studies.

general_safety.name: Turmeric and curcumin
general_safety.short: Case series link turmeric supplements to liver injury, sometimes severe. Curcumin may alter levels of some drugs, including anticoagulants, mostly in non-clinical studies.

products.name: Ginger
products.summary: One double-blind randomized controlled pilot trial was found in PubMed searches on 25 November 2026. Forty-five people with IBS took placebo, 1 g of ginger or 2 g of ginger a day for 28 days. Response rates were 57.1% with placebo, 46.7% with 1 g and 33.3% with 2 g, so ginger did not perform better than placebo. The trial was small, and its authors said larger trials are needed before firm conclusions can be drawn. The abstract does not report IBS subtype.
products.safety_interactions: In the pilot trial, side effects were mild and were reported by 35.7% of the placebo group and 16.7% of the ginger groups. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited study.

general_safety.name: Ginger
general_safety.short: Pregnancy trials found no significant rise in miscarriage (with wide uncertainty), heartburn or drowsiness. A warfarin review flags possible added bleeding risk.

products.name: Prebiotics and synbiotics
products.summary: A 2019 meta-analysis of 11 randomized trials in 729 people with IBS or other functional bowel disorders found no difference between prebiotics and placebo in response (54% versus 63%, a comparison that rests on response data from 191 people: 52 of 97 versus 59 of 94), or in abdominal pain, bloating or quality of life, and none of the trials was at low risk of bias across all categories. Type mattered: inulin-type fructans made flatulence worse. A 2026 fibre meta-analysis found no significant overall effect on symptom scores except for galacto-oligosaccharides, which improved symptoms (2 of the included trials tested them). For synbiotics (a probiotic combined with a prebiotic), a 2024 network meta-analysis found no significant improvement, and two other meta-analyses said the data were too sparse to judge.
products.safety_interactions: In the 2019 meta-analysis, inulin-type fructans worsened flatulence compared with placebo. Other adverse events and interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited abstracts.

general_safety.name: Prebiotic fibres
general_safety.short: Fructooligosaccharides, one prebiotic fibre, are highly fermentable and may cause bloating and flatulence; a meta-analysis of eight trials found no more gut symptoms than in comparison groups.

general_safety.name: Probiotics
general_safety.short: Trials have not shown increased risk, though safety reporting is weak. Rare bloodstream infections occur, mainly in people who are severely ill, immunosuppressed or in intensive care.

products.name: St John's wort
products.summary: In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 70 people with IBS (29% constipation-predominant, 37% diarrhoea-predominant, 31% mixed) took St John's wort or placebo for 12 weeks. Both groups improved, and the placebo group had significantly lower bowel symptom scores at 12 weeks. The authors concluded that St John's wort was less effective than placebo.
products.safety_interactions: No safety data found in the cited trials.

general_safety.name: St John's wort
general_safety.short: Induces drug-metabolising enzymes and lowers levels or effect of many medicines (e.g. warfarin, cyclosporin, digoxin, oral contraceptives). Serotonin syndrome reported with SSRI antidepressants.

products.name: Wheat bran (insoluble fibre)
products.summary: A 2014 meta-analysis of randomized trials found no effect of bran on IBS symptoms, and a 2015 meta-analysis found insoluble fibre did not improve any outcome. In a 12-week placebo-controlled trial of 275 people in primary care, bran did better than placebo in the third month only, and that result was not statistically significant in the worst-case analysis; symptom severity after three months did not differ from placebo.
products.safety_interactions: In the 275-person trial, early dropout was most common in the bran group, mainly because IBS symptoms worsened. The 2014 meta-analysis did not find evidence of harm from bran. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited studies.

general_safety.name: Wheat bran
general_safety.short: In irritable bowel syndrome trials, bran was worse than placebo for wind-related symptoms and less well tolerated than another fibre. No interaction data were found.

products.name: Senna
products.summary: Senna is a stimulant laxative. No randomized or observational studies of senna in people with IBS, including constipation-predominant IBS, were found in PubMed searches on 25 November 2026. Evidence from chronic constipation without IBS does not count for this page.
products.safety_interactions: No safety data found in the cited trials.

general_safety.name: Senna
general_safety.short: A case report links years of heavy use to liver failure; chronic abuse may cause fluid and electrolyte loss. A review found no convincing evidence of a link with colon cancer.
